scenes.name: Motown: Supremes y Holland-Dozier-Holland
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los grupos de Tamla/Motown ocuparon el hueco de los girl groups: Martha and the Vandellas («Heat Wave», «Dancing in the Street», «Nowhere to Run»), Gladys Knight, las Marvelettes, las Velvelettes y, sobre todo, las Supremes, el grupo pop americano de más éxito del momento (seis números 1 en dos años). Tres amigas del proyecto Brewster-Douglass, las «Supremes sin éxitos» hasta «Where Did Our Love Go» (1964): Berry Gordy vio en ellas el caballo de Troya para entrar en el mercado blanco, con los Funk Brothers, la escritura «psicológica» de Holland-Dozier-Holland (playlets femeninos sobre el amor como adicción, música dura contra letras sumisas) y el departamento de Artist Development de Maxine Powell y Cholly Atkins. Su imagen de espectáculo (Copacabana, pelucas) contrastaba con la nueva bohemia rock, como en su incómodo encuentro con unos Beatles fumados. Diana Ross ardía: seis números 1 y aún las trataban como a un grupo cualquiera.

podcast.title: Advocacy for Brian Holland
podcast.body: In his early time with Barry Gordy, Eddie frequently tried to convince Gordy to take his younger brother Brian seriously, despite Brian being in his early teens and Gordy's skepticism about his talent. "Eddie spent much of his early time working with Gordy, trying to get Gordy to take his little brother seriously."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 111: "Heat Wave" by Martha and the Vandellas

podcast.title: Dislike of Live Performance
podcast.body: While Eddie Holland loved singing, he strongly disliked the experience of performing on stage. Despite this, he continued performing, believing it was important not to quit a job until a better opportunity arose. "Holland quickly found that he didn't enjoy performing on stage. He loved singing, but he didn't like the actual experience of being on stage."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Singing Career & Jackie Wilson Comparison
podcast.body: Years before Motown's start, Eddie Holland worked with Barry Gordy as a singer. He was known for a voice similar to Jackie Wilson's, and Gordy initially hired him as a demo singer for songs intended for Wilson, later attempting to mold him into a "Wilson clone" with his first single, "You." "He was a singer who was known for having a similar sounding voice to that of Jackie Wilson, and Gordy had taken him on, first as a sound-like demo singer, recording songs written for Wilson, so Wilson could hear how they would sound in his voice, and later trying to mold him into a Wilson clone, starting with Holland's first single, You."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Motown Tour Guide
podcast.body: Eddie Holland, a member of the renowned songwriting trio Holland-Dozier-Holland, personally guided Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff through Motown's facilities on Gamble's first plane journey, providing them with insights into the music industry, including how contracts functioned. "Eddie Holland, who was part of the legendary songwriting trio, Holland Dozier Holland with his brother Brian and Lamont Dozier, showed them around."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Part of Holland-Dozier-Holland
podcast.body: Eddie Holland, Brian Holland's brother, became a new writing partner for Brian, along with Lamont Dozier, effectively forming the renowned Holland-Dozier-Holland songwriting and production team. "Freddie kept finding that when he came round to hit the film after work, if Brian Holland had had an idea for a song, he'd already finished it, usually with the help of his brother ready and their new writing partner, Lamont Dozier."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Songwriting Technique - Repeat Formation
podcast.body: Eddie Holland developed a songwriting technique he called "repeat formation" after studying Smokey Robinson's writing. He aimed for lyrics where every word mattered, without meaningless filler. To ensure the song's idea was conveyed even if a line was misheard, he would paraphrase the same piece of information two or three times within the lyrics. "So he came up with a technique he referred to as repeat formation, where he would give the same piece of information two or three times, paraphrasing it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Switch to Songwriting for Royalties
podcast.body: After his minor hit "Jamie" failed to earn him royalties (due to unearned production costs), but his brother Brian showed a royalty statement for thousands of dollars from songwriting, Eddie realized he was in the wrong job. He disliked performing and was earning nothing, so he took nine months off to teach himself songwriting, only performing the bare contractual minimum. "Eddie decided that he was in the wrong job. He didn't like performing anyway, and his brother was making serious money while he was working away earning nothing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
